clinicalPearls: A defect in the diaphragm allows abdominal viscera to herniate into the thorax during fetal development, impairing lung growth; the posterolateral (Bochdalek) defect, more often left-sided, is most common.
The principal problems are pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension rather than the anatomical defect itself.
Many cases are detected on antenatal ultrasound, allowing delivery at a centre with neonatal surgical and intensive care support.
A typical presentation is respiratory distress soon after birth with a scaphoid (sunken) abdomen and a shifted apex or heart sounds, and reduced breath sounds on the affected side.
Bowel sounds may be audible in the chest, and the chest radiograph shows bowel loops in the thorax with mediastinal shift.
Bag-mask ventilation should be avoided because it distends the herniated bowel and worsens lung compression; early endotracheal intubation and gastric decompression are preferred.
Initial management focuses on gentle, lung-protective ventilation, cardiorespiratory stabilisation, and treatment of pulmonary hypertension before surgery.
Surgical reduction and repair of the defect is undertaken after the infant is physiologically stabilised, not as an emergency.
Severe cases may need advanced support such as inhaled pulmonary vasodilators or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation.
reference.pathophysiology: Failure of the diaphragm to close completely during embryogenesis permits abdominal organs to occupy the thoracic cavity while the lungs are developing. The space-occupying viscera restrict growth of the ipsilateral (and to a lesser extent contralateral) lung, producing pulmonary hypoplasia with fewer alveoli and abnormal, muscularised pulmonary arterioles. After birth these abnormal vessels fail to relax normally, causing persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting, hypoxaemia, and acidosis. The combination of reduced functional lung tissue and elevated pulmonary vascular resistance drives the respiratory failure that dominates the clinical course.
additionalDifferentials: Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Antenatal ultrasound and, where available, fetal MRI with lung volume estimation
Chest and abdominal radiograph showing thoracic bowel loops and mediastinal shift
Echocardiography to assess pulmonary hypertension and exclude associated cardiac lesions
Blood gas and pre- and post-ductal oxygen saturations to gauge shunting
Evaluation for associated anomalies and genetic conditions
redFlags: Severe respiratory distress and hypoxaemia at or shortly after birth
Persistent pulmonary hypertension with right-to-left shunting refractory to therapy
Deterioration after bag-mask ventilation distends intrathoracic bowel
Signs of inadequate oxygenation and rising acidosis
Associated major cardiac or other anomalies worsening the outlook
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends chiefly on the degree of pulmonary hypoplasia and pulmonary hypertension and on associated anomalies. With optimal perinatal care many infants survive, though survivors may have chronic lung disease, feeding and growth problems, and neurodevelopmental sequelae. Severe hypoplasia and refractory pulmonary hypertension carry a poor prognosis.
pitfalls: Using bag-mask ventilation and inflating herniated bowel, worsening lung compression
Rushing to surgery before stabilising pulmonary hypertension and gas exchange
Attributing neonatal distress to primary lung disease and missing the diagnosis on examination and radiograph
Using aggressive high-pressure ventilation that risks barotrauma to hypoplastic lungs
Overlooking associated cardiac and genetic anomalies that affect management and prognosis
management: Secure the airway at birth with elective endotracheal intubation, avoiding bag-mask ventilation, and decompress the stomach with a nasogastric tube
Ventilate with a gentle, lung-protective strategy accepting permissive hypercapnia to minimise barotrauma to the hypoplastic lungs
Treat persistent pulmonary hypertension with inhaled nitric oxide and pulmonary vasodilators, escalating to extracorporeal membrane oxygenation for refractory hypoxaemia
Support the circulation with fluids and inotropes or vasopressors and correct acidosis
Undertake delayed surgical repair of the diaphragmatic defect once the infant is physiologically stabilised
Deliver and manage at a centre with neonatal surgery and intensive care, considering foetal tracheal occlusion in severe antenatally diagnosed cases
Evaluate for associated anomalies and genetic conditions, and provide long-term follow-up for chronic lung disease, feeding and growth difficulties and neurodevelopmental sequelae
